intro:
Hecker must get through — 20 April 1848

Dear Friend, I have only time for a few lines. Hecker is negotiating with General von Gagern, but the federal troops demand an unconditional surrender. We have too few men to hold here if the talks fail.

Our orders are to bring Hecker safely east and find the supporters waiting along the Rhine and Neckar. We must leave before the troops close around us. The rising will need its people more than it needs this patch of ground.

intro:
Hecker's uprising — 20 April 1848

Dear Friend, we are marching for a German republic. Volunteers are gathering in the towns, and the German Democratic Legion is approaching from the south. At last it feels as though our little column belongs to something larger.

We are to secure the towns around the Neckar and bring the force together for an advance on Freiburg. Enemy troops are approaching from the east, so the roads behind us must stay open. Karlsruhe will have to wait until we have the strength to reach it.

Hecker's assembly point is at position 29,29; he must join the march there.

intro:
The Palatinate uprising — 13 June 1849

Dear Friend, the Palatinate has risen, and we have joined the fight again. Prussia is sending experienced troops against us. Their guns and discipline will be difficult to face in open country, however much courage our volunteers bring.

We are to take the towns that can support the rising and defend the routes between them. More volunteers may join where we establish control. The hills give us a chance to hold the Prussians while the new men are organised.

But there's very good news, too ! The People of Baden and their whole army, except the High Command, has joined again our side!
Now, we must retreat to Baden, and unite our armies....

intro:
Waghausel — 21 June 1849

Dear Friend, the Prussians have pushed us back across the Rhine. Baden's soldiers have joined the revolution, but enemy forces are closing from several directions and there is little room left behind us.

We must hold the positions around Waghausel and keep the army together. The new troops give us strength; they also need time to find their places in the line. If we are driven apart here, there may be no army left to defend the republic.

intro:
The St. Louis Arsenal — 10 May 1861

Dear Friend, for years our battles seemed far away. We taught, printed newspapers, built clubs and raised families here. Now Missouri is divided, and I am taking up arms again. I did not cross the ocean to see another man's freedom treated as property.

Our German volunteers need weapons, and the arsenal at St. Louis is the first task. Secure it and reopen the northern supply connections. There can be no proper re-equipment until those stores and roads are in our hands.

intro:
Boonville — 17 June 1861

Dear Friend, we have drawn modern weapons and are marching west from St. Louis. The Missouri carries men and supplies across the state; while the State Guard holds Boonville, that route remains insecure.

We are to take the town and clear the positions overlooking the river, with a ship supporting the advance. The opposing troops are still organising. My old sergeant says we should reach them before they have time to become an army.

intro:
Wilson's Creek — 10 August 1861

Dear Friend, Sigel has proposed a movement we remember from the German fighting: Lyon will engage the enemy in front while our column comes in behind. If the two attacks meet, we may break the force threatening our hold on Missouri.

We are to turn the enemy's rear and seize the positions along our advance. Hold what we take until the main force reaches us. Losing our last foothold would leave this detached column with nowhere to stand.

intro:
The hemp bales at Lexington — 20 September 1861

Dear Friend, the hospital at Anderson's House is full and the canteens are almost empty. The spring is under fire. Now the State Guard is rolling wet hemp bales towards our works, and our shots do little to stop that moving shelter.

We are to hold Masonic College, the hospital and the approaches north of Lexington. There may be a chance to recover ground in the town, but first the line must survive the next assault. Every position abandoned brings their rifles closer to the wounded.

intro:
Pea Ridge — March 1862

Dear Friend, we are carrying the advance into Arkansas. The forces immediately ahead appear weak, but reports say Van Dorn is bringing another army towards them. What looks like a pursuit could become a battle on two fronts.

Take the positions around Pea Ridge and keep the enemy groups from joining. We need control of these approaches before their combined strength can turn us back towards Missouri.

intro:
Kernstown — 23 March 1862

Dear Friend, our march has brought us into the Shenandoah Valley. Its roads lead towards the Potomac, and Jackson's force can draw troops away from the main Union advance merely by threatening them.

We are to hold the Kernstown line while a second group takes Glasshouse to the west, then bring both groups against the Confederate positions. Our old flanking manoeuvre will be of little use if one column attacks before the other is ready.

intro:
Retreat at Bull Run — 28 August 1862

Dear Friend, the enemy has turned our flank. Confederate troops are coming from the south, and the attack has begun before we can finish drawing back. The roads towards Washington must not be left open behind a broken army.

Our orders are to withdraw into the defensive positions and hold the whole line. Keep the columns moving through one another without losing their organisation. This will be harder than advancing: someone must always remain facing the pursuit.

intro:
Harpers Ferry — 15 September 1862

Dear Friend, Harpers Ferry lies where two rivers meet beneath wooded heights. It is a beautiful place for a town and an alarming place to find oneself surrounded. The railway junction makes it too important to abandon lightly.

We are to defend the town and, if the opportunity opens, take Maryland Heights and threaten Jackson's headquarters at Keller. My sergeant says he can smell Confederates whichever way the wind blows. Today I believe him.

Fredericksburg — December 1862 (fictional force composition)

Dear Friend, the engineers are laying bridges across the Rappahannock. Beyond Fredericksburg the Confederate guns overlook the roads and railway from the heights. We have been ordered across that river and up those slopes.

The corps has received four regiments of Black infantry. They will share the assault with the men who have followed us since Missouri. We must find a way onto the heights without leaving successive regiments alone under the same batteries. I have rarely disliked the look of an order more.

intro:
Chancellorsville — 2 May 1863

Dear Friend, we are waiting in country they call the Wilderness. The woods hide everything beyond the next bend, and our scouts have lost contact with the enemy's main body. A quiet road here tells us very little.

Headquarters orders us to hold the line. Keep the approaches watched and the neighbouring formations in contact. If the Confederates come through these woods, there may be little warning before they are among the forward posts.

intro:
Vicksburg — 19 May 1863

Dear Friend, we are back beside the Mississippi. Vicksburg holds the river from its heights; beyond it, Port Hudson is the other remaining barrier to a Union passage. Opening the river would divide the Confederacy's eastern states from those to the west.

We are to take Vicksburg and secure the De Soto peninsula, with cavalry operating on the eastern approaches. The USS Moose has been assigned to the corps. Keep her with us: a gunboat that knows this river is worth more than another few rifles ashore.

intro:
Gettysburg — 1 July 1863

Dear Friend, what began as a report of Confederate scouts is becoming a battle. Lee's army is close, and the troops around Gettysburg have only just taken their positions. Our corps was meant for another direction, but there is no question where it is needed now.

Bring the men up to strengthen the line, especially the Codori Heights. Enemy reinforcements are expected from the west; our own are coming from the east and south. The first task is to hold long enough for those scattered columns to become one army.

intro:
Bristoe Station — 14 October 1863

Dear Friend, we have marched all day towards Manassas Junction, and now the firing ahead is growing. The Confederates have struck II Corps without realising how close our own column is behind it.

Repel the attack from the north and keep the army moving along the railway towards the withdrawal points. The passage must carry our men and the neighbouring formations, not just the first regiments to reach it. Leave a covering force until the tail of the column is clear.

intro:
Charleston — February 1864 (fictional assault)

Dear Friend, after a week aboard ship we finally know our destination: Charleston. Some troops are already ashore in the southern swamps, and our corps is to join them in an attack on the port. Most of the men would welcome any order that brought them onto dry ground.

The harbour forts cover the landing routes. Use the fleet to keep their guns occupied while the troops establish a foothold and advance on the city. We need Charleston itself; do not let every outlying battery draw the landing force into a separate siege.

intro:
New Market — May 1864

Dear Friend, Sigel is with us again. Over a drink we counted the years since the Rhine, but there was little time for old stories. Breckinridge is gathering troops against our advance through the Shenandoah Valley, including cadets from the Virginia Military Institute.

Our march is meant to protect the Union railway connections and break the Confederate ones. Clear the positions around New Market and secure the roads beyond them. We are deep in enemy country, with no neighbouring column close enough to rescue an isolated advance.

intro:
Harpers Ferry — 4 July 1864

Dear Friend, Early's approach has brought us back to Maryland Heights. Sigel withdrew the troops north of the Potomac rather than leave them trapped in Harpers Ferry. From here we can see the bridges we have been ordered to recover.

Retake the town and its crossings. The riverfront is defended; look for a passage that brings the troops onto the approaches instead of straight under the enemy's guns. We need the junction open again, with a force able to hold both banks.

intro:
Mobile Bay — 5 August 1864

Dear Friend, the voyage from New Orleans has brought us to Mobile Bay. The siege engineers aboard were a good clue: our task is to take the forts guarding the entrance and open the bay to the fleet.

The ships will bombard the positions before the troops land on the islands. Bring the landing parties ashore while the batteries are occupied. The old Moose is still with us; give her time to reach her place before the faster ships carry the attack ahead.

intro:
Petersburg — 25 October 1864

Dear Friend, Petersburg's railways feed Richmond, and our army still holds only the eastern approaches. The crater left by the earlier mine is a warning of what another unsupported frontal assault would cost.

We are to extend the siege west and take the connections supplying the town. Reinforcements are coming from the east, with cavalry approaching from the south-east. Use them to close the routes that keep the Confederate army here; the fall of those junctions would threaten Richmond as well as Petersburg.

intro:
Fort Fisher — 13 January 1865

Dear Friend, we are off the Cape Fear River. Fort Fisher guards the naval approaches, and our corps is to land north of it while another force works towards the western positions. The fleet will support us, but Confederate vessels are still reported upriver.

Take the fort and the bases it protects. Bring engineers with the landing troops, and keep the ships to waters they can navigate. More naval support is coming. The Black regiments marching with us know as well as anyone what opening this coast may mean for the people still held in slavery beyond it.

intro:
Close the trap — 1 April 1865

Dear Friend, Sigel has returned to command the cavalry, and new regiments have joined us after Fort Fisher. Around Petersburg the rains have swollen the rivers. The men joke that their next battle will be fought from gunboats, but the Confederate attack on our line has already begun.

Hold against that assault, then advance on Petersburg and the ground south of the Appomattox. Our cavalry must help close the remaining roads. Lee's army knows what losing them would mean and will fight to keep a way out.

intro:
The key to Richmond — May 1865 (alternate history)

Dear Friend, Petersburg has fallen, but the Confederate government and army are still holding Richmond. Some of our men are already celebrating. Those of us studying the James River forts have put the celebration aside.

Advance north and take Drewry's and Chaffin's Bluff, securing the Richmond and Petersburg Railroad. Captured locomotives and river steamers can carry the heavy equipment, and our marines hold a bridgehead at the western ferry. Open the approaches so the whole corps can come against the capital.

intro:
Final assault on Richmond — June 1865

Dear Friend, we are outside Richmond. The troops who began with us in Missouri have been joined by men who were enslaved when this war began. I think of the road from Germany whenever I look along their line.

Our orders are to enter the city and take the remaining Confederate positions. Marines, infantry and cavalry will reinforce the attack; keep the river passages open for them and draw battered regiments out before they are spent. I hope my next letter can tell you we are coming home.

briliant.text:
Final Assault at Richmond * BV

----{secret telegraph depeche to general}-----
THE WHITE HOUSE; WASHINGTON,

Dear Sir,
Unbelievable, you made it !!!
You have taken Richmond and the enemy had to surrender !
The war is over ! We have won !
if you plan to run for presidency in the future, I could help you with advice...
God bless and long live liberty !

THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES
-----{end of secret telegraph depeche}----

dear friend,
we have won, I fullfilled my duty: I resign as general, return to my school and teach young people again.....
there is one thing that I will teach them for sure: Their are times where freedom must be defended....
and here my friend, here ends my long journey to freedom.
